Lead story

Ray: Okay, so here's the setup. Velo3D and Sandia National Laboratories say they plan to explore whether different metal printers can reproduce the same part.

Ray: And I want to be upfront. For this one, we only have the headline and a short note. There's no paper and no results yet. So this is about the problem, not a finding.

Ada: Fair. So why is the problem hard?

Ray: Because most results we see come from a single machine. Someone tunes a printer, makes a nice part, and publishes. But showing that the part comes out the same on different machines is a much harder test. Settings that work on one printer don't automatically carry over to another.

Ada: And is there a control? Like, the same part, same powder, same settings on every machine?

Ray: Not stated. So treat this as a lead to watch. If the data does get published, a cross-printer comparison would be one of the more useful things in the field.

Magnets and materials

Ray: On to the magnets and materials desk. First, a systematic comparison of how you pick training data for molecular and materials property prediction.

Ada: Meaning, which examples are worth paying to label?

Ray: Yes. They compared random sampling against several active learning strategies, across different models, datasets, and target properties. The abstract says the best choice depends strongly on the model, the dataset, and the task. But uncertainty-based sampling generally did best.

Ada: So, not a magic bullet, but a decent default.

Ray: That's a fair reading. Next, a related one on scaling. Researchers trained three machine-learned interatomic potentials, M three G N E T, MACE, and PET, on growing subsets of a pool of about one point one six million structures.

Ada: Interatomic potentials being the fast models that stand in for expensive quantum calculations.

Ray: Right. Error falls as a power law with more data. But the exponent and the error floor depend on the architecture, the target, the sampling policy, and the test set. Rankings can even reverse on a distribution-shifted test set, and embedding-diversity sampling often did worse than random.

Ada: That's a little humbling. The abstract is cut off, though?

Ray: It is, so the final conclusions are unconfirmed.

Ray: Last one. A paper on a nanocrystalline, multi-main-phase neodymium cerium iron boron magnet. The title claims better magnetic properties and thermal stability from grain-boundary design.

Ada: Claims being the operative word.

Ray: Yes. We only have the title and author list, no abstract, so no numbers. But cerium-containing magnets are part of the push for cheaper alternatives to neodymium-rich designs.

Metal printing

Ray: Metal printing now, and this one's good. Researchers grew single-crystal CMSX four nickel superalloy using laser directed energy deposition, in long cylindrical rods.

Ada: Single crystal is notoriously finicky. What did they do?

Ray: They adjusted laser power dynamically, using infrared thermal feedback during the build, and added a simulation-guided external cooling system. That kept conditions near steady state at the solidification front, and extended single-crystal growth to nearly twice the height from process control alone.

Ada: And how do we know it's actually single crystal?

Ray: Electron backscatter diffraction, which maps crystal orientation. They also saw near-constant primary dendritic arm spacing, which points to steady solidification. Bonus, they cut the solutionizing heat treatment time by forty seven percent.

Ada: Closed loop, checked against real metallurgy. Nice. Caveat, it's directed energy deposition, not powder bed.

Ray: Right. Next, neural operator surrogates for keyhole melt pool simulations. They trained three model types on FLOW three D WELD simulations, which cost from one to thousands of core hours per track.

Ada: Is this experiment or simulation?

Ray: Simulation only. Temperature error is under two percent on straight tracks, and about five percent with two to four beams. Inference takes under a second per time step. Predicted keyhole depths landed within thirty percent of published measurements.

Ada: Thirty percent is loose, so it's a fast physics stand-in, not a sensor replacement.

Ray: Agreed. And one more headline. GKN Aerospace reports a world-first Nadcap approval for wire laser directed energy deposition. Nadcap is an aerospace special-process accreditation. Details are unconfirmed beyond the headline.

Ray: Okay, my favorite corner. The central limit theorem says sums of random things look Gaussian. But at a critical point, correlations are long range, and that breaks the rule. So does any general law survive?

They used local checks to detect errors, and ran up to fifteen Trotter steps, in a regime where classical tensor networks struggle.

Velo3D and Sandia to test cross-printer part reproducibility

News · AM policy & funding · 8/10

Only the headline is available: Velo3D and Sandia plan to explore whether different metal printers can reproduce the same part. Showing that a part comes out the same on different machines is a hard test that single-machine results rarely address. Whether the effort will publish in-process sensor data or only final part outcomes is not yet known.

Far tails of critical Ising fluctuations collapse onto one law

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports using Tethered Monte Carlo on the 2D Ising class to probe rare fluctuations of the order parameter, down to probabilities near 10^-200. Once normalized by width, the tails collapse onto a single asymptotic law shared by different microscopic models, with a universal amplitude compatible with a conformal-field-theory conjecture. It is a rare-event view of critical behavior, but the method relies on tethering and is specific to 2D.

Potts-type order preempts a U(1) spin liquid in 3D vorticity models

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports that entropy-driven height locking, mapped to a 3-state Potts antiferromagnet, stops a 2-form spin liquid from forming in pyrochlore and related lattices. All three models undergo a 3D Ising transition, while pinch points persist at intermediate scales. The result shows that pinch-point signatures can coexist with weak underlying order.

Neural-operator surrogates trained on keyhole melt-pool simulations

arXiv · ML for manufacturing · 6/10

The abstract reports FNO, RIGNO and GAOT surrogate models trained on FLOW-3D WELD simulations, with under 2% temperature error on straight tracks and about 5% for multi-beam paths. For held-out conditions, predicted keyhole depths fall within 30% of published measurements. The work is simulation-only and checked against literature rather than experimental sensor data, so it is best read as a fast physics surrogate.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Uncertainty-based sampling generally wins in training-data acquisition study

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports a systematic comparison of random sampling and active-learning strategies for molecular and materials property prediction. Effectiveness depends strongly on the model, dataset and task, though uncertainty-based sampling generally did best. It is a useful reference for choosing which data to label when each label is expensive to compute.

MLIP scaling exponents depend on architecture, sampling and test set

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

The abstract reports power-law data scaling for M3GNet, MACE and PET, but exponents and error floors vary, and sampling-policy rankings can reverse on a distribution-shifted test set. Embedding-diversity sampling often underperformed random sampling. The takeaway is caution for foundation-model-driven screening, though the text is cut off, so the final conclusions are unconfirmed.

Nd-Ce-Fe-B magnet study claims gains from multi-main-phase grain-boundary design

J. Magnetism & Magnetic Materials · 5/10

The title claims better magnetic properties and thermal stability in a nanocrystalline, multi-main-phase Nd-Ce-Fe-B magnet. Cerium-containing permanent magnets are part of the push for lower-cost alternatives to neodymium-rich designs. No abstract is available, so the results are unconfirmed.

LLM agent screens a 15-million-entry DFT database for materials

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract describes Alexandria, a database of about 15 million DFT calculations, paired with a generative model, a universal potential and property-prediction GNNs, all handed to a general-purpose LLM agent. The agent screens for a solar absorber and flags an unreported Ba-Zr-S sulfide. It is a template for AI-driven materials screening, though the abstract does not mention magnetic properties.

Additive Manufacturing

Infrared feedback keeps single-crystal CMSX-4 superalloy growing in laser deposition

arXiv · AM monitoring & physics · 6/10

The abstract reports dynamic laser-power adjustment from in-situ infrared feedback, plus simulation-guided cooling, extending single-crystal growth to nearly twice the height reached with process control alone. EBSD was used to validate the single-crystal structure. It is closed-loop monitoring checked against real metallurgical results, though in a nickel superalloy using directed-energy deposition rather than powder-bed fusion.

Physics-guided multi-output learning for wire-arc additive manufacturing of aluminium

News · AM policy & funding · 5/10

The title points to interpretable, physics-guided multi-output learning for circular-path cold metal transfer wire-arc printing of ER5356 aluminium alloy. No abstract is available, so the details are unconfirmed. It is a possible example of interpretable process modeling, though it uses wire-arc rather than laser or powder-bed methods.

Formnext 2026 preview covers AM simulation, monitoring and inspection

News · AM policy & funding · 5/10

3DPrint.com previews monitoring and inspection tools ahead of the Formnext trade show, but only the headline is available. It offers a sense of where vendors are showing sensing and inspection products this year.

GKN Aerospace earns world-first Nadcap approval for wire laser-DED

News · AM policy & funding · 6/10

The headline calls this a world-first Nadcap approval for wire laser directed-energy deposition. Nadcap is an aerospace special-process accreditation, so the approval marks a qualification milestone. Details are unconfirmed, and the process is specific to aerospace.

Theoretical Physics

Pinch-point structure factor for Ising spins on the centered pyrochlore

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract reports a generalization of Henley's method to inequivalent center and vertex spins, in excellent agreement with Monte Carlo simulations. It captures sharp and broadened pinch points at finite temperature. The result gives researchers an analytic benchmark for spin-correlation analysis on frustrated lattices.

Functional RG for non-polar structural transitions in O(d) models

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract reports an O(d) model with an extra kinetic term, relevant to dipolar and spin-orbit-coupled magnets. It finds the extra coupling irrelevant at the Wilson-Fisher fixed point, so quantum-to-classical correspondence re-emerges. The abstract is cut off, so the full conclusion on corrections is unconfirmed.

63-qubit processor watches electric flux strings in a 2+1D gauge theory

arXiv · quantum physics · 6/10

In plain words, confinement means charges are joined by a flux string that cannot be pulled apart. The abstract reports a superconducting processor evolving such strings with dynamical matter, using local Gauss-law checks for error detection. Classical tensor-network methods struggle here as entanglement grows, so this shows quantum hardware reaching dynamics that classical computers cannot easily follow.

Gravitational waves hint that failed supernovae make ~10-solar-mass black holes

APS Physics · 5/10

The idea in plain words is that some massive stars may collapse straight into black holes without a visible explosion. The APS summary says this could explain the surprising number of merging black holes near 10 solar masses. It matters because it links black-hole populations to how stars die, but only a short summary is available, so the strength of the evidence is unconfirmed.
